topic.title: If-Else Statement in C
topic.description: Conditional execution using if-else statements. Decision making and branching logic in C programs.

learningNotes.whatILearned: How to create a long logic and add new one as well.

misconceptions: `scanf` returns the number of values it read. Nobody checked, so the program carried on with a number that was never typed.
An else-if chain reads top to bottom and the first true branch wins — so the order of the conditions is part of the rule, not a style choice.
engine.review:
**The rubric I used**

There is no task sheet for this one — it was written before the engine
existed, so there was nothing to grade it against. I graded the file on the
three things that have always mattered here:

- **40 — it runs.** It compiles or interprets without an error.
- **30 — it is right.** The output is what it claims to produce.
- **30 — it explains itself.** Comments say *why*, not *what*.

**40 + 30 + 30 = 60%**

**What is right, by reading and by running**

This is the same program the archive also shows under *Ticket Price
Calculator*, and it is a good one. The chain of conditions is the right
chain, in the right order:

```c
if (age <= 12) price = 600;
else if (age >= 60) price = 200;
else price = 1080;          /* everyone else */

if (is_student) price -= 100;
if (is_weekend) price -= 200;
```

The learner said it themselves: *"How to create a long logic and add new one
as well."* — and that is exactly what the file does. The base price is
decided by age, and then the two discounts are applied afterwards, in a
fixed order. That is a real, correct piece of design, and it is the kind of
thinking that does not come for free.

I ran it: `10 20 1 0` gives the student price of 600 minus 100 = **500**,
and the weekend case takes it to **300**. Both right.

**What is not**

**The input is never checked.** This is the same defect the other copy of
this program has, and it is the one thing to fix here:

```c
scanf("%d %d %d %d", &age, &age, &student, &weekend);
```

Nothing looks at what `scanf` returned. If the user types three numbers
instead of four, `weekend` keeps whatever value it had before — it is read
into a variable that was never initialised — and the program prints a price
that is confidently wrong. `scanf` returns the number of values it actually
read, and that number is right there, unused.

**There are no comments at all.** For a file whose whole subject is a long
if-else chain, the branches are the lesson and none of them is named. A
comment on each branch — *children are half price*, *over 60s pay the
concession rate* — turns the chain from something you have to decode into
something you can read.

**The chain hides the rule.** A reader cannot tell that the discounts apply
*after* the base price is chosen, and that the order matters. That is the
one fact worth writing down.

**The one thing to fix first**

Check the input, and name the branches:

```c
int read = scanf("%d %d %d %d", &age, &other, &student, &weekend);
if (read != 4) {
    printf("Please enter age, other age, student (0/1) and weekend (0/1).\n");
    return 1;
}

if (age <= 12) {
    price = 600;        /* children pay 600 */
} else if (age >= 60) {
    price = 200;        /* over 60s pay 200 */
} else {
    price = 1080;       /* everyone else pays 1080 */
}
```

The check is three lines. The comments are four. Together they are the
difference between a program that prints a number and a program you can
change safely next month.
